GO NOW OR STOP SOON - an e-scooter entrepreneur fights for a share of the road in Stellenbosch

By: Marion Edmunds | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Tonight we get stuck in a traffic jam in Stellenbosch - as traditional traffic bosses seek to close down an e-scooter entrepreneur

Unique Selling Point:
We will show Stellenbosch stuck at a crossroads - between embracing electric mobility or sticking to traditional ways to manage traffic congestion - either by building new roads or forcing residents to wait in long traffic jams at their intersections. We have unique access to the founder of the e-scooter company, Jacob Levitan, and the date he has collected. His scooters are wildly popular with students, and takes mobility in the town on trend globally. But they leave the local traffic officials scratching their heads, and digging in their heels, while older residents fume at what they perceive to be feral unlicensed modes of transport.

Summary:
GoNOW or StopSOON?
How a pioneering electric scooter start-up is being pushed off the streets of Stellenbosch
For the past five years, a homegrown electric scooter start-up, GoNOW, has quietly transformed how thousands of students and residents move through Stellenbosch — offering cheap, safe, app-based transport in a town choking on traffic.
Now, just as fuel prices threaten to skyrocket amid global tensions (Iran war) and Stellenbosch hits daily gridlock across three peak rush hours, the municipality is moving to shut the service down — citing vague, unnamed complaints.
This is the story of innovation colliding with bureaucracy.
It begins with 19-year-old Capetonian Jacob Levitan, who imported the idea of app-based electric scooters from Europe and launched in Stellenbosch with municipal support. At the time, officials were actively encouraging non-motorised transport as the town expanded rapidly — with new developments, rising tourism, and a swelling student population of around 30,000, many now bringing cars of their own each term.
Levitan started with 100 scooters. The town adapted. Demand grew.
Two years later: 200 scooters.
Today: 500.
They now clock between 40,000 and 50,000 trips a month — criss-crossing Stellenbosch day and night. For students, they’re more than a convenience: they’re freedom. A lift to class when you’ve overslept. A safer ride home after a night out. A way to beat congestion entirely.
The system is simple: download the app, unlock a scooter, ride within a geo-fenced area, and leave it at your destination. Each night, teams collect and redistribute them. The model is efficient, scalable — and, until recently, embraced.
Schools like Rhenish Girls’ High have even approached GoNOW to install dedicated scooter parking, citing improved safety for learners traveling to extra murals. Levitan has years’ worth of unsolicited thank-you messages from users who say the scooters have changed their daily lives.
But in late February, everything shifted.
Levitan received an email from the municipality referencing complaints — with no detail. When he asked to meet, there was silence. Then, suddenly, an ultimatum: present yourself within two hours or face mass impoundment of all scooters.
At the eventual meeting — attended by Traffic Chief Gavin Solomons and, curiously, the Head of Procurement — Levitan was told the scooters could be impounded due to complaints and a lack of legislation governing electric vehicles of this kind.
While the legal gap is real, officials refused to disclose the complaints: how many, from whom, or what the issues were.
After four years of operation, the business now faces an existential threat — with no clear explanation.
Behind the scenes, Levitan has been told the push may be coming from the mayor’s office. He suspects the programme could be repositioned as a municipal tender — raising questions about whether innovation is being sidelined for control or profit. ( I am not sure whether he will say that on camera – but it’s a question we can ask)
At the heart of the story is a bigger issue: South Africa has no clear regulatory framework for emerging electric mobility. GoNOW has effectively been operating as a real-world pilot — a transport guinea pig — in a country increasingly desperate for affordable, local alternatives as fuel costs rise.
What happens in Stellenbosch could set a precedent nationwide.

Tone & treatment:
Energetic, visual, and slightly irreverent. The presenter experiences the entire story on a scooter — moving through the town, linking from key locations, and immersing viewers in the very transport solution now under threat.
In many ways it’s a story about whether South Africa really has an appetite for electric mobility — and despite all the lip-service to non-motorised transport, whether innovation is being enabled or quietly shut down.


Further information:
Stellenbosch is the first South African and possibly African town to host e-scooters but they are a phenomenon in other parts of the world, causing the same excitement but also the same headaches around safety and regulation. Spain has last month introduced a campaign to regularise the 4 million e-scooters there – which will force e-scooters to register their personal vehicles and buy in to a national road insurance scheme. South Africa’s law does not cover the use of e-scooters – strictly speaking they are illegal but their illegality stems from a regulation vacuum rather than an outright ban. The trend across these countries is that e-Scooters work best in places where there is already infrastructure for non-motorised transport like cycles, but works poorly in places where there is none.

Press Release:


GoNOW OR StopSOON?
In the Western Cape student town of Stellenbosch, electric mobility is rolling in to beat the traffic blues – but not everybody is happy about it. For four years, a homegrown electric scooter start-up has transformed how students and more adventurous residents travel through town. It’s efficient, scalable… and, until recently, embraced, especially by the under-30s. But now the municipality says it wants to shut the service down. South Africa has no clear regulatory framework for emerging electric mobility. So, as innovation collides with bureaucracy, what happens in Stellenbosch could set a precedent nationwide. Should this e-scooter start up really go now, or must it stop soon?
Producer: Marion Edmunds | Presenter: Catherine Rice

Script:


(Catherine Rice) Stellenbosch: a picture-perfect postcard of oak trees and academia. But beneath the leafy canopy, the town is choking. Every day, thousands of cars back up in extended rush-hours.

(Wikus van Niekerk) It sometimes takes the staff of the university more than half an hour just to do three blocks to get out of town. It is absolutely horrendous.

(Catherine Rice) The traffic is a growing crisis.

(Tracey Megom) Total gridlock. And it can take 20 to 30 minutes to actually drive around the corner.

(Catherine Rice) But for a young entrepreneur it was an opportunity.

(Jacob Levitan) I just jumped into the deep end and saw, you know, a problem, and thought, I think I have a solution for this.

(Catherine Rice) For the thousands of people who live and work in this town, these multiple rush hours aren’t just frustrating, they are eating into their fuel, their time and their sanity.

(Catherine Rice) In response, electric battery-powered scooters are rolling out as a mode of last-mile transport. While some scooters are privately owned, the majority belong to a single rental service called Go Now which has become increasingly controversial among the townsfolk. Student Inge van der Westhuizen says they arrived unannounced four years ago, littering the pavements.

(Inge van der Westhuizen) One night there was nothing, and the next night, the streets were filled with scooters. And I think we were all a bit apprehensive at first about it, but then once I tried it for the first time and we had fun on it, yeah, we were all quite keen about the idea. I don’t know, it does feel a little bit like you're flying.

(Catherine Rice) But while the students were flying to class, some residents were seeing red. The Dean of Engineering at Stellenbosch University, Professor Wikus van Niekerk, still sees an e-scooter accident waiting to happen on the busy streets.

(Wikus van Niekerk) There's a huge safety risk on these scooters. The roads are fairly narrow, and we've got these water furrows next to the road, so they're in between the traffic. They wear no helmets, right. I know that they are quite nippy in some sense, so they actually, they entice you to nip between the cars.

(Catherine Rice) To take a ride, download the app, create an account and then locate the nearest scooter on the map. Then pay for a pay-per-minute or monthly package, scan the QR code and it’s ready to roll.

(Catherine Rice) No petrol. No parking battles. And no sitting in traffic. And I’m going to give it a go.

(Upsound Catherine Rice) Wow! Ok! This is actually really fun.

(Catherine Rice) Next stop is the entrepreneur behind this popular service who is astonishingly only 22 years old. After school, when his friends went to university, Jacob Levitan tagged along and while they swotted, he set up a rental e-scooter company.

(Jacob Levitan) I saw a real problem in the town was traffic congestion. And not only that, but friends were often late to class. So scooters were really a no brainer.

(Catherine Rice) Jacob has spent the last four years tweaking his service to allay safety concerns. At Rhenish Girls High School, the Head, Tracey Megom, was alarmed at how e-scooters were piling up at their gate and she called Jacob into her office.

(Tracey Megom) I mean, we arrived at school one morning, there were 17 scooters parked outside our school gate. So we engaged with him, and he was very open to that engagement. I must say, I was impressed. And then he immediately blocked the school off on the app, it's now a red zone so you can't drive the scooters into the school property anymore. And he's now created a specific parking zone on the pavement outside the school. I think if you park the scooter anywhere else, then you get a fine.

(Catherine Rice) Tracey was won over. But Wikus is not.

(Wikus van Niekerk) If the scooters are no longer in town, everybody will be better off. I do not think it's an appropriate transport solution for Stellenbosch.

(Catherine Rice) And in agreement is the town’s traffic chief who this year threatened to confiscate the Go Now fleet. The municipality declined an interview with us, but claims in writing that e-scooters are illegal. Transport Planner and part-time Stellenbosch resident Richard Gordge says the conflict could be resolved with a bylaw.

(Richard Gordge) The challenge really is where do e-scooters operate, pavement-based or road-based, or a combination of what speeds, and just how to manage those interactions with other road users. These are challenges, they're not insurmountable, and it's really important for South Africa to start addressing how we can accommodate these innovators.

(Catherine Rice) Gordge consults in Europe where many cities and towns are integrating e-scooters into the flow of traffic, while regulating the way they are ridden. For example in Spain, helmets are mandatory.

(Richard Gordge) Typically, what happens is that the mode grows in use, until it becomes a real established kind of user in the urban space, and then the legislation catches up.

(Catherine Rice) In the absence of rules of the road, Jacob is attempting to self-regulate his service through the Go Now software.

(Jacob Levitan) Our scooters work on a system called geo fencing. It's a technology that allows us to create a digital map with digital zones around a town in your service area, which speak to the scooters.

(Catherine Rice) Go Now has ringed Stellenbosch with a geo-fence: any scooter that goes beyond this boundary will automatically stop. Jacob also uses the tech to slow the scooters down on busier roads. A scooter trip is still four to five times quicker than walking.

(Jacob Levitan) Top speed of our scooters is 25 kilometres an hour, and 22 kilometres an hour in winter season for safety, and then they slow down to as low as 13 kilometres an hour in certain areas around the map

(Catherine Rice) This isn’t just a scooter service: it’s a data-driven system. Every route, every stop, every ride is tracked. And that tells a much bigger story – not just about scooters – but about how this town actually moves.

(Catherine Rice) The 500 scooter Go Now fleet is averaging 40 to 50 thousand trips a month, and most users are students. Those we have spoken to are fans of Jacob’s service and his entrepreneurial spirit. Student Noah Chego rents a room off-campus and has become one of Go Now’s regulars.

(Noah Chego) So I have done 2147 rides, and then I have used 1101 kilometres.

(Catherine Rice) So it’s really changed your life?

(Noah Chego) That’s a long distance yeah, I use scooters almost every day.

(Catherine Rice) Even headlines reflecting e-scooter fatalities in other parts of the world don’t scare the students off. Writing for the campus newspaper, Die Matie, Inge tried to find examples of e-scooter accidents in town.

(Inge van der Westhuizen) Through my research, a lot of people are like: Oh yeah, my friend's cousin's sister was like hit by an idiot in the scooter. And then you try to pursue and they're like: Oh no, but I don't really know what happened there. So I've heard a lot of gossip, but I haven't gotten a lot of concrete evidence about anything that I can say with certainty: it happened or not.

(Catherine Rice) Go Now has hired a security team to police reckless riding.
Jacob says the injury record speaks for itself.

(Jacob Levitan) To my knowledge, we haven't heard of any serious injuries, anything more of a sprained ankle or a bloody knee.

(Catherine Rice) It’s a stand-off. Despite the threats, Go Now scooters are still on the road. But the municipality says it’s are consulting lawyers to get them removed.

(Tracey Megom) I think I would be a little bit angry about that. I can only support somebody who's going to come up with an entrepreneurial idea, and there’s a need, and I think if the municipality are willing to engage, then I think they can make it work.

(Catherine Rice) Back at headquarters, Jacob is standing firm. He now employs twenty staff who keep the scooters tidy and swap out the growing number of charged batteries.
Jacob says the lessons he’s learnt are important because Go Now could be a test case for e-scooters on other South African streets.

(Jacob Levitan) I believe it gives us the opportunity to be a leading role model of a company, for how electric transport and electric scooters could be an electric transport service in the future.

Jacob also uses the tech to slow the scooters down on busier roads. A scooter trip is still four to five times quicker than walking. (Jacob Levitan) Top speed of our scooters is 25 kilometres an hour, and 22 kilometres an hour in winter season for safety, and then they slow down to as low as 13 kilometres an hour in certain areas around the map (Catherine Rice) This isn’t just a scooter service: it’s a data-driven system. Every route, every stop, every ride is tracked. And that tells a much bigger story – not just about scooters – but about how this town actually moves. (Catherine Rice) The 500 scooter Go Now fleet is averaging 40 to 50 thousand trips a month, and most users are students. Those we have spoken to are fans of Jacob’s service and his entrepreneurial spirit. Student Noah Chego rents a room off-campus and has become one of Go Now’s regulars. (Noah Chego) So I have done 2147 rides, and then I have used 1101 kilometres. (Catherine Rice) So it’s really changed your life? (Noah Chego) That’s a long distance yeah, I use scooters almost every day. (Catherine Rice) Even headlines reflecting e-scooter fatalities in other parts of the world don’t scare the students off. Writing for the campus newspaper, Die Matie, Inge tried to find examples of e-scooter accidents in town. (Inge van der Westhuizen) Through my research, a lot of people are like: Oh yeah, my friend's cousin's sister was like hit by an idiot in the scooter. And then you try to pursue and they're like: Oh no, but I don't really know what happened there. So I've heard a lot of gossip, but I haven't gotten a lot of concrete evidence about anything that I can say with certainty: it happened or not. (Catherine Rice) Go Now has hired a security team to police reckless riding. Jacob says the injury record speaks for itself. (Jacob Levitan) To my knowledge, we haven't heard of any serious injuries, anything more of a sprained ankle or a bloody knee. (Catherine Rice) It’s a stand-off. Despite the threats, Go Now scooters are still on the road. But the municipality says it’s are consulting lawyers to get them removed. (Tracey Megom) I think I would be a little bit angry about that. I can only support somebody who's going to come up with an entrepreneurial idea, and there’s a need, and I think if the municipality are willing to engage, then I think they can make it work. (Catherine Rice) Back at headquarters, Jacob is standing firm. He now employs twenty staff who keep the scooters tidy and swap out the growing number of charged batteries. Jacob says the lessons he’s learnt are important because Go Now could be a test case for e-scooters on other South African streets. (Jacob Levitan) I believe it gives us the opportunity to be a leading role model of a company, for how electric transport and electric scooters could be an electric transport service in the future.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Tonight we get stuck in a traffic jam in Stellenbosch - as traditional traffic bosses seek to close down an e-scooter entrepreneur
metadata.Unique Selling Point: We will show Stellenbosch stuck at a crossroads - between embracing electric mobility or sticking to traditional ways to manage traffic congestion - either by building new roads or forcing residents to wait in long traffic jams at their intersections. We have unique access to the founder of the e-scooter company, Jacob Levitan, and the date he has collected. His scooters are wildly popular with students, and takes mobility in the town on trend globally. But they leave the local traffic officials scratching their heads, and digging in their heels, while older residents fume at what they perceive to be feral unlicensed modes of transport.
metadata.Summary: GoNOW or StopSOON? How a pioneering electric scooter start-up is being pushed off the streets of Stellenbosch For the past five years, a homegrown electric scooter start-up, GoNOW, has quietly transformed how thousands of students and residents move through Stellenbosch — offering cheap, safe, app-based transport in a town choking on traffic. Now, just as fuel prices threaten to skyrocket amid global tensions (Iran war) and Stellenbosch hits daily gridlock across three peak rush hours, the municipality is moving to shut the service down — citing vague, unnamed complaints. This is the story of innovation colliding with bureaucracy. It begins with 19-year-old Capetonian Jacob Levitan, who imported the idea of app-based electric scooters from Europe and launched in Stellenbosch with municipal support. At the time, officials were actively encouraging non-motorised transport as the town expanded rapidly — with new developments, rising tourism, and a swelling student population of around 30,000, many now bringing cars of their own each term. Levitan started with 100 scooters. The town adapted. Demand grew. Two years later: 200 scooters. Today: 500. They now clock between 40,000 and 50,000 trips a month — criss-crossing Stellenbosch day and night. For students, they’re more than a convenience: they’re freedom. A lift to class when you’ve overslept. A safer ride home after a night out. A way to beat congestion entirely. The system is simple: download the app, unlock a scooter, ride within a geo-fenced area, and leave it at your destination. Each night, teams collect and redistribute them. The model is efficient, scalable — and, until recently, embraced. Schools like Rhenish Girls’ High have even approached GoNOW to install dedicated scooter parking, citing improved safety for learners traveling to extra murals. Levitan has years’ worth of unsolicited thank-you messages from users who say the scooters have changed their daily lives. But in late February, everything shifted. Levitan received an email from the municipality referencing complaints — with no detail. When he asked to meet, there was silence. Then, suddenly, an ultimatum: present yourself within two hours or face mass impoundment of all scooters. At the eventual meeting — attended by Traffic Chief Gavin Solomons and, curiously, the Head of Procurement — Levitan was told the scooters could be impounded due to complaints and a lack of legislation governing electric vehicles of this kind. While the legal gap is real, officials refused to disclose the complaints: how many, from whom, or what the issues were. After four years of operation, the business now faces an existential threat — with no clear explanation. Behind the scenes, Levitan has been told the push may be coming from the mayor’s office. He suspects the programme could be repositioned as a municipal tender — raising questions about whether innovation is being sidelined for control or profit. ( I am not sure whether he will say that on camera – but it’s a question we can ask) At the heart of the story is a bigger issue: South Africa has no clear regulatory framework for emerging electric mobility. GoNOW has effectively been operating as a real-world pilot — a transport guinea pig — in a country increasingly desperate for affordable, local alternatives as fuel costs rise. What happens in Stellenbosch could set a precedent nationwide. Tone & treatment: Energetic, visual, and slightly irreverent. The presenter experiences the entire story on a scooter — moving through the town, linking from key locations, and immersing viewers in the very transport solution now under threat. In many ways it’s a story about whether South Africa really has an appetite for electric mobility — and despite all the lip-service to non-motorised transport, whether innovation is being enabled or quietly shut down.
metadata.Further information: Stellenbosch is the first South African and possibly African town to host e-scooters but they are a phenomenon in other parts of the world, causing the same excitement but also the same headaches around safety and regulation. Spain has last month introduced a campaign to regularise the 4 million e-scooters there – which will force e-scooters to register their personal vehicles and buy in to a national road insurance scheme. South Africa’s law does not cover the use of e-scooters – strictly speaking they are illegal but their illegality stems from a regulation vacuum rather than an outright ban. The trend across these countries is that e-Scooters work best in places where there is already infrastructure for non-motorised transport like cycles, but works poorly in places where there is none.
